name: Black peel (Chinese peel)

lead: Black peel is an in-clinic chemical peel made from black acetic acid with salicylic acid and other actives. It is used to clear acne and even out skin tone.
In a 2024 split-face study it reduced acne lesions by about 58%, about the same as 25% TCA, with less burning and redness.

paras: The acids exfoliate the upper skin layers in a controlled way so the skin renews. A clinician applies it to light frosting and rinses it off; sessions were two weeks apart in the trial.

Reported effects were mild burning, redness and sometimes dryness or flaking; no pigment problems occurred in the small trial. Peels in general can cause pigment changes or scarring, more so when deeper.

web.title: Black peel vs 25% TCA split-face study (full text)

chain: Chemical exfoliation of the upper skin layers
Fewer acne lesions and more even pigment
angle.text: Black peel is applied in a clinic to exfoliate the skin. In one study it reduced acne lesion counts by about 58% over three sessions, and a case report describes lightening of facial hyperpigmentation. People use it to get clearer, more even skin.

lead: Black peel, sometimes called a Chinese peel, is a dermatology-clinic chemical peel used to improve acne, uneven pigmentation and skin texture. The version described in the medical literature is a superficial-to-medium-depth formulation that combines black acetic acid with salicylic acid, tetrahydrojasmonic acid, biosulfur and potassium iodide.[1] People looking to clear breakouts, fade dark patches such as melasma, or smooth the face use it as a gentler-feeling alternative to some other peels, and it is applied by a clinician in the office.[2][3]

The black acetic acid component is described in the literature as a traditionally produced fermented vinegar from Japan and Korea.[4] Published research is small but real. A 2018 case report described a single session with several passes in a woman with facial hyperpigmentation, framed around peels that improve appearance without prolonged recovery or surgery.[2] A 2024 split-face study of 30 people with mild to moderate acne compared black peel on one side with 25% trichloroacetic acid (TCA) on the other, over three sessions two weeks apart.[1]
infobox: Chinese peel, black acetic acid combination peel
Black acetic acid, salicylic acid, tetrahydrojasmonic acid, biosulfur, potassium iodide[1]
Three sessions two weeks apart in one trial[1]

paras: Black peel has been studied for acne vulgaris and for facial hyperpigmentation including melasma.[1][2] Melasma is a chronic pigment disorder of sun-exposed skin, and the case report places black peel among treatments sought for its cosmetic and psychological impact without the risks of surgery.[2]

Earlier small studies cited by the 2024 trial authors include a Korean preliminary study of 13 patients (2012) and an Indian study of 20 patients with nodulocystic acne who had poor compliance with isotretinoin (2019); both reported lower acne grades after three sessions.[4]

The formulation studied contains 50% black acetic acid, 0.5% salicylic acid, 6% tetrahydrojasmonic acid, 10% biosulfur and 0.1% potassium iodide.[1] In the 2024 trial, patients were pre-treated with sunscreen and tretinoin 0.025% for two weeks, a patch test was done behind the ear, and the peel was applied with a cotton-tip applicator to light frosting, then rinsed with water without needing neutralization.[1][4] After each session, patients were told to avoid soap for 24 hours and to avoid sun exposure and reapply sunscreen.[4]

The trial authors describe jasmonic acid as exfoliating the epidermis and regulating sebaceous activity, salicylic acid as loosening dead cells and reducing inflammatory pathways, biosulfur as keratolytic and antibacterial, and potassium iodide as antibacterial.[4] Chemical peels in general work by controlled injury that prompts skin to shed and renew.[3]

In the 2024 split-face study (30 patients aged 15 to 45), mean total lesion reduction was 57.74% on the black peel side and 57.59% on the 25% TCA side, with no significant difference between sides.[1] Global assessment rated good improvement in 86.7% of black peel sides and 80% of TCA sides.[1]

Burning or stinging was reported in 10% of black peel sides versus 20% of TCA sides and post-peel redness in 6.7% versus 16.7%; desquamation and dryness were seen only on the TCA side, and no post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was seen on either side.[1][4] The authors noted the small sample and the use of a non-standardised grading scale, and described TCA as a cost-effective alternative.[4] The 2018 case report described a single session in a woman with facial hyperpigmentation.[2]

Chemical peels in general can cause redness, stinging, peeling, pigment changes and, with deeper peels, scarring, and the risk rises with depth.[3] In the black peel trial no major adverse effects occurred; the reported effects were mild burning, stinging and redness.[1][4]
Black peel appears in skin-focused discussion as one of several in-clinic peel options, sometimes called a Chinese peel, alongside TCA and glycolic peels.[3]
